title: EFFECTS OF OFFICE LIGHTING ON MOOD AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE AND A GENDER EFFECT IN WORK-RELATED JUDGMENT
research_question: To investigate (a) the mood-mediated effects of recommended office lighting (color temperature) on subjects' intellectual performance, and (b) gender effects in a performance appraisal task, considering both rater and ratee gender.

participants.description: Eighty participants (40 males, 40 females) from a local college of health sciences, aged 18 to 55, were randomly assigned to one of two luminous milieus.
participants.recruitment: recruited from a local college of health sciences

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A controlled chamber (3.9 m × 3.8 m × 2.5 m) furnished as an off-white office. Air temperature and humidity were controlled. Six ceiling-mounted luminaries with four fluorescent tubes each provided two color temperature conditions: (a) 3000K (Osram, 36W, L36/32, CRI = 95) and (b) 4000K (Osram, 36W, L36/22, CRI = 95). Illuminance was stabilized at 1500 lux for 20-30 minutes before each session.

measures.instrument: 6 general knowledge questions based on a 7-page text about an ancient culture (Carter, 1982; Hygge, 1993)
18 multiple choice questions based on a 7-page text about an ancient culture (Carter, 1982; Hygge, 1993)
Recall of three 16-word lists (neutral, positive, negative hedonic tones) presented on a computer screen
Embedded figure task (Hartley, 1989) with 32 target figures
Performance appraisal task (Baron et al., 1992) with 10 rating scales (e.g., motivation, intelligence, overall evaluation) on a 7-point scale, for fictitious male and female bank clerks
Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) (Watson, Clark, & Tellegen, 1988) - 20 items, 5-point scale
Questionnaire (Knez, 1995a) - 7 items (glaring, dim, soft, bright, warm, intense, cool) on a 5-point scale

findings.antecedent: Office lighting color temperature (3000K vs. 4000K) and subject gender
findings.consequent: Change in positive mood (PANAS delta score)
findings.mechanism: 3000K (more reddish) and 4000K (more bluish) office lighting may communicate different affective loadings or meanings to each gender, with 3000K best preserving positive mood for males and 4000K for females.
findings.quote: The delta score analysis showed a strong tendency to a significant two-way interaction between gender and color temperature, F(1, 76) = 3.39, p = .06.

findings.antecedent: Cognitive workload (approximately 2 hours of intellectual work)
findings.mechanism: The cognitive workload induced by almost 2 hours of intellectual work diminished the subjects' positive mood.
findings.quote: The positive mood diminished in subjects over mood-blocks, albeit still high (from 30.2 to 27.6 on a scale ranging from 10.0 to 50.0).

findings.antecedent: Cognitive workload (approximately 2 hours of intellectual work)
findings.mechanism: The cognitive workload induced by almost 2 hours of intellectual work augmented a negative mood.
findings.quote: negative mood increased over mood-blocks, from 11.9 to 12.7

findings.antecedent: Office lighting color temperature (3000K vs. 4000K) and subject gender
findings.mechanism: 3000K lighting induced the least negative mood in males and 4000K lighting accounted for the same effect in females.
findings.quote: a two-way interaction between gender and color temperature, F(1, 76) = 4.48, p < .05.

findings.antecedent: Office lighting color temperature (3000K vs. 4000K)
findings.consequent: Performance on free recall, long-term recall, and recognition tasks

findings.consequent: Performance on embedded figure task (problem solving)
findings.quote: Only the main effect of gender was significant, F(1, 76) = 5.24, p < .05. Compared to females, males performed significantly better (21.5 vs. 17.0 out of 32.0).

findings.consequent: Ratings on performance appraisal task dimensions

findings.mechanism: Females are more expressive (in general terms) toward the indoor lighting (an affective source) than are males.
findings.quote: females perceived the room light as significantly more glaring than did males

findings.antecedent: Office lighting color temperature (3000K vs. 4000K) and subject gender
findings.mechanism: Females perceived 3000K lighting as less warm than 4000K, while males perceived 3000K as more warm than 4000K. This suggests gender-specific affective loadings or meanings of color.
findings.quote: females evaluated the 3000K lighting as less warm than the 4000K lighting. The opposite result, however, was yielded for males.

findings.antecedent: Office lighting color temperature (3000K vs. 4000K) and subject gender
findings.mechanism: Females estimated 4000K lighting as less cool than 3000K, while males evaluated 4000K lighting cooler than 3000K. This suggests gender-specific affective loadings or meanings of color.
findings.quote: females estimated the 4000K lighting as less cool than the 3000K lighting, and by contrast, males evaluated the 4000K lighting cooler than the 3000K lighting

mechanisms: Different color temperatures (3000K reddish, 4000K bluish) communicate different affective loadings or meanings to each gender, potentially acting as a 'mnemonic device' triggering culturally specified and affectively based meanings of color, thereby altering mood.
Cognitive workload induced by prolonged intellectual work (approximately 2 hours) significantly influences subjects' moods, diminishing positive mood and augmenting negative mood.
Raters' processes of judgment in performance appraisal tasks are significantly biased by the demographic variable of the ratee's gender.
moderators: Gender (as a moderator for lighting effects on mood and light perception)
implementation_implications: Current recommendations for general ceiling-mounted office lighting (CIE, 1986) may need to consider individual requirements, particularly gender-specific preferences for color temperature, as lighting can act as a mood inducer.
Performance appraisal tasks should be used with caution in applied real-world contexts due to demonstrated bias based on the ratee's gender.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of Office Lighting on Mood and Cognitive Performance And A Gender Effect in Work-xRelated Judgment
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of Office Lighting on Mood and Cognitive Performance And A Gender Effect in Work-xRelated Judgment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The study presents an investigation of the effects of the recommended office lighting on subjects' mood and cognitive performance in the physical setting of an office. In addition, a gender effect in the performance appraisal task was examined, both as a between-and within-subject factor. The results showed no significant effect of the lighting on the performance of cognitive tasks. However, an interaction between gender and color temperature on mood showed that 3000K (more reddish) and 4000K (more bluish) office lighting may communicate different affective loadings or meanings to each gender. The cognitive workload induced by almost 2 hours of intellectual work diminished the subjects' positive mood and augmented a negative mood. Moreover, independently of their gender, the raters evaluated the neutral female significantly different from the neutral male ratee. Implications of these findings for the mood effects of indoor lighting and the gender effect in work-related judgment are discussed.
